episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Science, Wonder & the Natural World
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Science, Wonder & the Natural World.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is trust something you build, or something you inherit?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down School District 27 preliminary election results announced and Lab-grown brains can now read Braille and guide robot dogs, plus 6 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Does a record or scientific claim earn public belief, and who controls the data and decisions behind it? Topics include: Planetary vital signs and the choice of indicators, Australian High Court ruling on scope 3 emissions and the Mount Pleasant mine, US fossil fuel buildout and electricity demand from data centres, Glacier and landslide hazards in Alaska and monitoring continuity in the Cariboo, Denisovan fossil research and community trust in science.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society

discussion.central_question: Does a record or scientific claim earn public belief, and who controls the data and decisions behind it?
discussion.riley_position: Riley argues that quantified evidence like the planetary vital signs and the High Court ruling deserves belief, and that institutions fixing their blind spots, with records published and auditable, show that numbers can earn trust.
riley_key_evidence: Seven of sixteen planetary vital signs are at the most extreme values recorded, with CO2 about 50 per cent above preindustrial levels
Warming rate rose from about 0.05 C per decade (1880-1970) to about 0.36 since 2010
The Australian High Court ruled 3-2 that Mount Pleasant mine planners had to account for scope 3 emissions
discussion.casey_position: Casey argues that numbers are only as trustworthy as the choice of indicators and the people who control them, and that community trust depends on who sets questions, reads records, and inherits monitoring.
casey_key_evidence: The 44 per cent figure is a share of indicators chosen by the authors, not a planetary forecast, and changing the list moves the share
The scope 3 ruling focused on only about 2 per cent of the project's emissions, showing a planning loophole
The Denisovan study's method is only as good as its comparison set, and most readers never reach the caveats
discussion.resolution: They did not fully agree. Riley conceded that good news needs a baseline and that publishing raw series and methods lets people audit claims, while Casey agreed that the test of local knowledge setting the question matters but noted a single pass is only a receipt, not a relationship. They left the question of trust open, with Riley trusting the instrument and Casey focused on who gets to read it.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE
These analytical threads were identified before generation. Use the findings to ground Riley's and Casey's arguments with real evidence. Develop them as substantive exchanges, not a citation list. Cite naturally.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Do the 2026 BioScience "state of the climate" findings hold up, and what is the "reason for hope" that the coverage highlights?
Findings: The paper is "The 2026 state of the climate report: challenges and opportunities" in BioScience (lead author Bill Ripple, Oregon State University; 11 authors including Johan Rockström of PIK in Germany). Of 16 tracked planetary vital signs (greenhouse gases, temperatures, oceans, ice, energy balance, wildfire), 7 (44%) are at record extremes. Coverage notes several others are trending in the wrong direction and some show acceleration or abrupt shifts. The reporting also frames "signs of positive change" alongside the warnings, so the report is not purely doom. The publication date is reported as October 14 in some outlets, while WIRED describes it as published on a Wednesday. Treat the exact date as something to confirm before citing it.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue that a count of vital signs is itself a success story, since it shows we can measure the system closely enough to spot shifts early, and that the "positive change" findings prove interventions are working. Casey can push on what "record extreme" means for a 16-indicator dashboard. Indicator selection, baseline choices, and the fact that a 44% share is a headline rather than a forecast all deserve scrutiny. Casey can also ask whether a "patient" metaphor (Ripple's quote) pushes readers toward fatalism or toward action.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What did Australia's High Court actually rule on the Mount Pleasant/Hunter Valley coal mine, and how far does the precedent reach?
Findings: The High Court of Australia ruled 3–2 on October 7, 2026 that the NSW Independent Planning Commission failed to consider imposing conditions to ensure greenhouse gas emissions are "minimised to the greatest extent practicable." The ruling turned on scope 3 emissions (the coal's downstream combustion). The commission had focused on only about 2% of the project's emissions, per the reporting. Campaigners, including a Hunter Valley community group, called it a landmark and a "binding national precedent." The Guardian reports that a NSW MP urged lawyers to challenge other coal approvals. Legal commentary (Verfassungsblog) describes it as a new frontier in project-based climate litigation, and it was decided on statutory language rather than a broad climate-duty finding.
Suggested angle: Riley can present this as proof that courts and existing law can force climate accounting into individual project approvals without new legislation, a sign that institutions are adapting. Casey can argue the ruling is narrow: it is a procedural failure under one state's planning law, it was a 3–2 split, and it requires authorities to consider conditions, not to refuse the mine. Casey can ask whether the mine will simply be re-approved with conditions. Both can use the 2% figure to debate whether emissions accounting in approvals has been a loophole.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the US fossil fuel buildout a "comeback," and what is driving it?
Findings: The Verge's report (framed as "The fossil fuel comeback is here") says the US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than in a decade, while renewable growth is slowing. Electricity demand is rising faster than in more than a decade, driven by data centers, factories, and EVs. Other coverage (Time) ties the trend to utilities turning back toward gas-fired plants to meet data-center demand. The Verge's framing ties this to federal energy policy under the Trump administration. I did not locate the underlying report's exact capacity figures in this search, so cite the trend qualitatively unless you verify the numbers.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue that AI and data-center demand is a genuine engineering problem, and that gas buys time and reliability while storage and nuclear scale up, so the "comeback" is a bridge rather than a retreat. Casey can counter that a bridge built to 30-year gas plants is a lock-in, and that "slowing renewables" is the more important signal. The debate can turn on whether data-center demand is a reason to build fossil capacity or a reason to question the demand forecasts themselves.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the "left-brained vs right-brained creativity" idea have scientific support?
Findings: Neuroscience does show some lateralization, meaning certain functions such as language are more concentrated in one hemisphere. However, a large resting-state connectivity study (researchers including Jared Nielsen) found no consistent pattern in which a whole "left-brain network" or "right-brain network" dominates in some people. Harvard Health and Dana Foundation commentary say the dominance idea is a misnomer: functions may be sharply divided in some brains and more evenly spread in others. Popular science debunkings (such as Dr Sarah McKay's) describe the theory as largely a myth. Creativity is generally understood as a network-level process involving memory, attention, and default-mode activity rather than a single hemisphere.
Suggested angle: This is a useful palate cleanser that shows how a folk idea can survive a century of contrary evidence. Riley can argue that brain-imaging tools are getting better at mapping individual variation, which is the wonder of the field. Casey can use the myth as a warning about how pop-science categories, personality quizzes, and career advice spread faster than data. Both can ask why the myth persists: it is intuitive, flattering, and easy to sell.

ELECTION RESEARCH: 2026 B.C. provincial general election

Background for the roundup's election stories and any race the hosts mention. It is not the deep dive's subject. The Williams Lake Tribune school trustee results were not used for any race below.

**FINDINGS: Cariboo-Chilcotin**

On the ballot: Kathryn Askew (BC NDP), Lorne Doerkson (Conservative), Douglas Gook (BC Green). Seat held going in by Lorne Doerkson.

- **Kathryn Askew (BC NDP).** The 100 Mile Free Press (Oct. 1, 2026) reports she is a retired school teacher from Canim Lake and was named the NDP candidate for Cariboo-Chilcotin. The BC NDP release names her as the riding's candidate and says she has 32 years in education, including leadership roles with the BC Teachers' Federation and her local union (bcndp.ca, undated in the copy read). The same release says she was the NDP candidate for Mission-Matsqui-Abbotsford in the 2025 federal election. Her result in that race is not established: the Fraser Valley Current results page read carried no figures, and a pre-nomination Mission City Record piece names a different NDP candidate. Her 2026 campaign results: My Cariboo Now (Oct. 24, 2026, at time of writing) reports 3,123 votes, second place. Victoria News (Oct. 24, 2026) reports about 17.1 per cent with 75 of 89 ballot boxes counted. No controversy involving Askew was found.

- **Lorne Doerkson (Conservative).** Sourced background (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19): MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin since 2020, first elected as a B.C. Liberal, re-elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative. BC Ballot (bcballot.ca, 2026 candidate page) gives his 2024 margin as 7,722 votes. Prior research, carried forward from Elections BC's 2020 statement of votes: 6,600 votes (51.25%) as a Liberal in 2020. Victoria News (Oct. 24, 2026) headlines his win as his "third time in a row" in the riding; the show has not established the details of the earlier election behind that headline. His 2026 result: My Cariboo Now (Oct. 24, 2026) reports 14,215 votes (77%) at time of writing; Victoria News (Oct. 24, 2026) reports 76.9% with 75 of 89 ballot boxes counted. The Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026, carried forward) reports he took over as Conservative leader; Victoria News (Sept. 23, 2026, carried forward) reports he is interim leader.
  - *Campaign controversy (allegation, columnist's assessment, not a finding):* Vaughn Palmer's Vancouver Sun column (Oct. 7, 2026, carried forward; paywalled in the copy read) says Doerkson told reporters he had made "no promises at all" on auto insurance, and argues he had made four. Palmer writes that Doerkson twice denied making commitments of any kind. Doerkson's response, as reported in that column, is the denial.
  - *Related party matters (not about Doerkson personally):* The Tyee (Oct. 8, 2026, carried forward) reports he fired the party's Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after social media posts the BC NDP flagged as racist. CityNews (Oct. 14, 2026, carried forward) reports a Conservative campaign director under fire over social posts will stay on, Doerkson says.

- **Douglas Gook (BC Green).** BC Green's candidate page (bcgreens.ca, 2026) lists him for Cariboo-Chilcotin and describes his forestry, reconciliation and environmental work. Elections BC's candidate report lists him for the riding. My Cariboo Now (Oct. 24, 2026) reports 1,103 votes at time of writing.
  - *Prior runs, as carried forward:* Caledonia Courier (Oct. 2024) reports he ran unsuccessfully four times as a Green candidate in North Cariboo, including a 2017 Nechako Lakes bid where he took about nine per cent. My Cariboo Now calls his 2020 bid his fourth run for the Greens in that riding. These two accounts do not reconcile the count of runs, and the show has not resolved it. Elections BC's 2020 statement of votes (carried forward) shows him at 707 votes (6.38%) in Cariboo North. CKPG Today (Sept. 13, 2024) announced him as the Green candidate for Nechako Lakes in 2024; his 2024 result is not established in the sources read.
  - No controversy was established.

**FINDINGS: Prince George-North Cariboo (includes Quesnel)**

On the ballot: Denice Bardua (BC NDP), Sheldon Clare (Conservative), Randy Thompson (BC Green). Seat held going in by Sheldon Clare. The Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports the three-candidate list was confirmed by Elections BC after nominations closed Oct. 3; CKPG Today (Oct. 3, 2026) lists the same three.

- **Denice Bardua (BC NDP).** CKPG Today (Sept. 24, 2024) reports she was announced as the NDP candidate in 2024. Her 2024 run: 3,426 votes, 17.0% (BC Ballot, Elections BC figures, 2024), finishing third behind Sheldon Clare and independent Coralee Oakes (4,394 votes, 21.8%). The Prince George Citizen (2026, undated in the copy read) also describes her as back on the ballot after a third-place finish with 17.03% in 2024. The earlier pass's "second place" description is incorrect: Oakes was second. The Prince George Citizen also describes her as an Indigenous education department secretary for School District 27. Her 2026 campaign result: the Prince George Citizen and My Cariboo Now (Oct. 24, 2026) carry the projected result; the Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 24, 2026) reports Clare projected to be re-elected. No controversy was established.

- **Sheldon Clare (Conservative, incumbent).** Sourced background (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19): won the riding for the B.C. Conservatives in 2024. Elections BC's 2024 statement of votes shows him at 11,430 votes, 56.82%. My Cariboo Now (Oct. 24, 2026) reports him declared MLA with over 10,000 votes, and the Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 24, 2026) reports him projected re-elected.
  - *Leadership bid (2026):* Times Colonist (Jan. 8, 2026, Canadian Press, carried forward) reports he said he was running for the B.C. Conservative leadership. CKPG Today (Jan. 20, 2026, carried forward) reports he formally launched the bid. CFJC Today (Feb. 28, 2026, carried forward) reports he suspended it, citing a leadership application issue in which some signatures were not accepted; he said he "takes full responsibility."
  - *Election-finance penalty (finding):* Elections BC's enforcement notice (March 30, 2026) and its April 1, 2026 release, as reported by CKPG Today (Apr. 1, 2026) and the Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Apr. 3, 2026), say he was fined $1,500 for accepting anonymous contributions for the 2024 election that exceeded the limit by about $4,000. Elections BC said the investigation found no deliberate attempt to circumvent the law. The Prince George Citizen reported the same penalty. His response to the penalty was not found in the sources read.
  - The prior pass's note on a September allegation was cut off in the copy received, so it is not carried forward here.

- **Randy Thompson (BC Green).** CKPG Today (Oct. 20, 2026) reports this is his second run for public office, the first being his 2024 bid for the same riding. He says he has served on the BC Green provincial council. The Prince George Daily News (Oct. 11, 2026) reports the party announced him as its candidate and says he is a farmer, small-business owner and municipal candidate; it also says he ran for the riding in the 2024 provincial election. His 2024 result: the Prince George Citizen (2026, undated in the copy read) reports 4.3% and fourth place; My Prince George Now (2024 live results) reports 848 votes (4.30%), last place. CKPG Today (Oct. 19, 2024) reports 790 votes (4.25%) on election night. No controversy was established. The CKPG Oct. 20, 2026 piece says Green candidates face harsh criticism on social media in general; that is his remark, not a specific incident.
